current_episode.title: S01 EP4 - Getting people on board with AI at work, with Charlotte Halligan

guest.bio_context: Charlotte Halligan has been working in internal communications for over 20 years, having experienced many different tech implementations and changes throughout her career. She describes herself as initially slow to adopt generative AI personally, but quickly came to see its real potential once she started using it. She took on a role where a major focus was rolling out generative AI tools at an enterprise level simultaneously with her own adoption journey, navigating a complex global organization with multiple types of roles, legislation, and regulations.

pending_qa.q: How should internal communicators approach the hearts and minds side of an AI rollout when traditional know-feel-do models fall short?
pending_qa.r: Charlotte found that the traditional know-feel-do sequence does not work well for AI adoption, and that starting with the 'do' piece was far more effective. She recommends creating fun AI-based activities for the first ten minutes of team meetings so employees play with the technology in a safe environment, building confidence that then builds capability in a virtuous cycle. She also emphasizes leaning on managers and people on the ground to tell the story rather than relying solely on senior leaders communicating centrally.

pending_qa.q: How should organizations communicate with frontline or production-line employees who feel existentially threatened by AI and automation?
pending_qa.r: Charlotte found that production-line staff were far more terrified of AI than, for example, finance teams, because they saw automation as an existential threat to their roles and understood that 'operational efficiencies' is often coded language for headcount reduction. She recommends spending dedicated time with those vulnerable groups, listening to their concerns without offering false reassurances, and being honest about the stakes. The framing she used was: it is not necessarily that AI is going to take your job, but somebody who knows AI is going to take your job.

pending_qa.q: Why is plain-English policy writing critical to psychological safety during an AI rollout, and what did reducing jargon actually achieve?
pending_qa.r: Charlotte's organization initially had an acceptable use policy that ran to seven pages filled with terms such as LLM, large language model, and prompt engineering — acronyms and jargon that immediately turned employees off. They cut that seven-page document down to two paragraphs in plain English, with a clear signpost for where to go for more information or specific questions. This shift was essential because the less confident people feel about the rules, the less willing they are to experiment safely.

pending_qa.q: What mistakes did Charlotte Halligan make during an enterprise AI rollout that others should avoid?
pending_qa.r: Charlotte identified three key mistakes: first, allowing clashing announcements — for example, headcount reduction notices going out at the same time as positive AI messages, causing employees to connect the two even when they were unrelated. Second, using too much tech jargon from the outset, such as the word 'prompts,' when plain language like 'ask your AI a question' would have been far more accessible. Third, having too many stakeholders with a voice in narrative development, which meant it took approximately six months into the rollout before a clear, locked-down key messaging framework was finally achieved.

pending_qa.q: How should organizations link their AI rollout narrative to company values and purpose rather than promoting AI for its own sake?
pending_qa.r: Charlotte argues that AI communication must be connected to the organization's values, purpose, and mission — and ideally to how responsible and economically viable generative AI usage helps the organization's customers achieve their goals. She warns that encouraging people to use AI simply to hit an adoption target, without finding where it genuinely adds value to the work being done, fails to tackle the underlying value problem. The golden thread linking AI to organizational purpose is the same principle that should underpin any internal communications campaign.

pending_qa.q: What is the risk of organizations that publicly championed AI then scaling back their usage due to cost or poor ROI?
pending_qa.r: Charlotte notes that some organizations are currently scaling back AI usage because the economic cost is becoming prohibitive and the ROI is not there, including reinstating customer service staff because AI tools failed to meet customer needs. She warns that scaling back after extreme public confidence in AI breeds cynicism among employees — particularly those who have seen many tech fads come and go. She advises communicators to use these external data points proactively with senior leaders to build honest, grounded narratives from the outset.
